title: 97. Quantitative Relationships & Measurement: Unit Rates from Tables
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.concept: Unit Rate from a Cost Table
questions.learningObjective: Determine the cost per notebook from a table of equivalent ratios.
questions.question:
The table shows the number of notebooks and their total cost.
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
\text{Notebooks} & 2 & 4 & 6\\
\hline
\text{Total cost (USD)} & 6 & 12 & 18
\end{array}
\]
What is the unit rate in USD per notebook?
questions.explanation: The unit rate is the cost for one notebook. Divide the total cost by the number of notebooks: \(6 \div 2 = 3\), \(12 \div 4 = 3\), and \(18 \div 6 = 3\). The unit rate is \(3\text{ USD}\) per notebook. The alternative reverses the quotient, giving the reciprocal numerical value; attaching the requested units does not correct that inversion.
questions.hint: Identify the quantity named after "per" and divide the other quantity by it, using one column.

questions.concept: Unit Rate from a Distance-Time Table
questions.learningObjective: Determine the speed in kilometres per hour from a distance-time table.
questions.question:
The table shows distance travelled and time taken.
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
\text{Distance (km)} & 100 & 150 & 200\\
\hline
\text{Time (h)} & 2 & 3 & 4
\end{array}
\]
What is the unit rate in kilometres per hour?
questions.explanation: The unit rate is the distance travelled in one hour. Divide the distance by the time: \(100 \div 2 = 50\), \(150 \div 3 = 50\), and \(200 \div 4 = 50\). The unit rate is \(50\text{ km/h}\). The alternative reverses the quotient, giving the reciprocal numerical value; attaching the requested units does not correct that inversion.
questions.hint: Identify the quantity named after "per" and divide the other quantity by it, using one column.

questions.concept: Unit Rate from a Mass-Cost Table
questions.learningObjective: Determine the cost per kilogram from a table of equivalent ratios.
questions.question:
The table shows the mass of rice and its total cost.
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
\text{Mass (kg)} & 3 & 5 & 8\\
\hline
\text{Cost (USD)} & 12 & 20 & 32
\end{array}
\]
What is the unit rate in USD per kilogram?
questions.explanation: The unit rate is the cost for one kilogram. Divide the total cost by the mass: \(12 \div 3 = 4\), \(20 \div 5 = 4\), and \(32 \div 8 = 4\). The unit rate is \(4\text{ USD}\) per kg. The alternative reverses the quotient, giving the reciprocal numerical value; attaching the requested units does not correct that inversion.
questions.hint: Identify the quantity named after "per" and divide the other quantity by it, using one column.

questions.concept: Testing a Table for a Constant Unit Rate
questions.learningObjective: Check whether every column has the same quotient.
questions.question:
A table shows the number of boxes and their total mass.
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
\text{Boxes} & 4 & 6 & 10\\
\hline
\text{Mass (kg)} & 10 & 15 & 26
\end{array}
\]
Does the table have one constant mass per box?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes; every column has the same mass per box.

options.label: B
options.text: No; the mass per box differs between columns.

questions.explanation: The first two columns give \(\frac{10}{4}=\frac{15}{6}=2.5\text{ kg}\) per box, but the last gives \(\frac{26}{10}=2.6\text{ kg}\) per box. Thus there is no single constant unit rate. Looking only at the first two columns would incorrectly accept the alternative.
questions.hint: Calculate the quotient in every column before deciding whether one rate fits the whole table.

questions.concept: Comparing Unit Rates Read from a Table
questions.learningObjective: Compare cost per kilogram using quantities supplied in a table.
questions.question:
The table compares two offers for nuts.
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{Offer} & \text{P} & \text{Q}\\
\hline
\text{Mass (kg)} & 2.5 & 4\\
\hline
\text{Cost (USD)} & 10 & 18
\end{array}
\]
Which offer has the lower cost per kilogram?
questions.explanation: Offer P costs \(\frac{10}{2.5}=4\text{ USD}\) per kilogram. Offer Q costs \(\frac{18}{4}=4.5\text{ USD}\) per kilogram. The lower unit rate belongs to P; the greater quantity in Q does not imply a lower unit price.
questions.hint: Divide the cost in each column by its corresponding mass.
